The last year of schooling will correspond to the first year of higher education under the current system. Therefore, higher education itself will become mainly a four-year programme.    In this way, we will move to a new twelve-year system and, at the same time, reduce the costs of this reform.    Of course, this will require preparation, which will take several years.    Therefore, during this time it is necessary to tighten up the lagging areas and seriously strengthen the material and technical base of the education system.    It is necessary, firstly, to start restoring the system of kindergartens and the formation of full-blooded preschool education. In the meantime, wherever possible, it is necessary to develop pre-school education at schools.    Secondly, one of the results of reforming the sector should be the emergence of a new generation of teachers.    I instruct the Government to increase the state educational order for teacher training by five thousand units from the 2005-2006 academic year.    Special attention should be paid to vacancies for teachers with polylinguistic education.    It is necessary to raise the qualification of teachers to a higher level of quality, strengthen the material and technical base of the Republican and regional retraining institutes for education system workers.    It is very important that teachers and children work in cosy schools and do not experience limitations in educational equipment, classrooms and sports grounds. In time, schools in Kazakhstan should rise to the level of the best world standards.    In the future, the teaching profession should become one of the most prestigious and highly paid. It goes without saying that the teacher himself should meet the requirements of the time.    Last year 68 schools were built, this year more than 70 new schools will be built, more than 500 schools will be renovated. This was not done even in the best years of our recent Soviet history.    At the same time, according to the most minimal estimates, we need to repair and build more than 1,900 more schools. This must be done in the next three years.    During the last 15-20 years, subject classrooms have not been practically renovated. We need to solve these problems during 2005-2008. This is the third most important task.    I instruct Akims of regions, Astana and Almaty cities to adopt regional programmes aimed at strengthening material and technical base of schools.    Akims (I want to emphasise the importance of this task) need to ensure that at least seventy-five per cent of schools are connected to the Internet as early as in 2005. The Government and akims should accelerate the task of telephoneisation of schools.    Fourth, children with developmental disabilities require serious attention. I instruct the Government together with akims to work out the issue of developing a network of boarding schools for this category of children.    Fifth, independent external assessment of students' academic achievements should be introduced to improve the quality of their knowledge.    The Government should complete the introduction of independent external control in the form of unified national testing of school leavers and interim certification of university students as early as this year. To provide institutional support for this important work, I instruct to create a National Centre for Education Quality Assessment.    Sixth, there are many complaints about the quality of textbooks. The government should conduct an inventory and a qualitative examination of them, and then take measures to remedy the situation.    Seventh, we must rethink the role of technical and vocational education.    The government, akims of all levels need to take effective measures aimed at developing a network of educational institutions of vocational technical education of young people, mainly with the involvement of one hour
This is the sector that needs these graduates.    Eighth, the network of domestic universities and branches of foreign universities remains redundant. The education they provide leaves much to be desired.    They should be reduced, including by tightening the requirements to the material and technical base and scientific and pedagogical staff.    Ninth, in the near future we will identify a small group of elite universities in the country, whose rectors will be appointed by the President, and the state will take an active part in their development.    These universities should become the benchmark for training specialists, including for the civil service.    And lastly. The country needs a new State Programme of Education aimed at the future.    The government should start developing it, involving the best domestic and foreign experts.    2.4 Social security

Social issues have been and will remain a priority for the state. The Law on Compulsory Social Insurance is to be enacted in 2005.    Next year it is necessary to index pensions ahead of inflation, setting the minimum pension at 6,200 tenge. The average size of pensions after the increase will be 9252 tenge.    More than 10.5 billion tenge will be allocated for pensions in 2005.    As I have already said, it is the sacred duty of the state to take care of those who are limited in their ability to work or have the same conditions for receiving income.    Helping these citizens is a reflection of the degree of humanisation and maturity of our society and is our duty. It is time and opportunity to fulfil it.    Starting next year, it is necessary to seriously increase state social benefits for disability and loss of breadwinner, allocating 15.8 billion tenge for these purposes. This will affect a total of more than 680 thousand people.    Benefits will be increased:    47 thousand disabled people of the first group - by 3 monthly calculation indices (by 2757 tenge) (MRP - 919 tenge);    More than 193 thousand disabled persons of the second group - by 2.5 MRP (by 2297 tenge);    Almost 125 thousand disabled persons of the third group will receive an increase in allowance by 2 MRP (by 1838 tenge);    More than 50 thousand disabled people under the age of 16 - by 3 MRP (by 2757 tenge);    262 thousand families who have lost a breadwinner will receive an increase in allowance up to one monthly calculation index.    As a result, in 2005, for more than 415 thousand disabled people, the average size of the state social security benefit will increase to 6,700 tenge, or by 50 per cent.    The average survivor benefit will increase by 20 per cent to 6500 tenge.    But these increases will not affect disabled people of all groups, who already receive maximum benefits. For them indexation will be carried out taking into account price growth.    There is another issue of our duty to our fathers and grandfathers, the issue of our historical memory.    Next year we will celebrate the sixtieth anniversary of the Victory in the Great Patriotic War and honour our dear veterans.    In connection with this significant date, in 2005 I instruct the Government to increase to 15 monthly calculation indices the amount of special state allowances for invalids and participants of the war and to provide veterans with one-time material support in the amount of 30 thousand tenge.    It is necessary to allocate 6.5 billion tenge for these measures.    On the whole, 217.2 billion tenge was allocated for social security at the expense of the national budget in 2004, covering more than 2.5 million people, and in 2005 the increase in expenditures for these purposes will amount to about 33 billion tenge.    Along with other measures to provide social support to low-income citizens, the number of people living below the poverty line should be reduced by more than half by the end of 2005 compared with the beginning of 2003.    We must also stimulate further population inflow into the country, so the immigration quota for Oralmans in 2005 should be increased to 15,000 families. For their resettlement and purchase of housing, 9.8 billion tenge should be allocated.    We will improve legislation to regulate labour relations, provide for incentives for legal employment in the Labour Code, and form a modern employment model.    Addressing the priority tasks of human development is extremely important.    Therefore, all regional development budgets should be used only for the development of education, health care, water supply and housing infrastructure.    In 2005, it is necessary to provide 15 billion tenge in the national budget for the construction of education, health care and water supply facilities in rural areas, and 5 billion tenge for especially important facilities in regional centres and cities.    * * *   Development of the social sphere and human resources is a key long-term priority for Kazakhstan.    The tasks I have announced are top-priority, but by no means exhaustive.    On my instructions, work is underway to strengthen the social orientation of reforms and to develop a new social policy.    It will be announced in a year.     3. Competitiveness of the state
  The competitiveness of the state is manifested in increasing the role and authority of the country in the international arena, in the ability of the state to solve the urgent problems of its citizens, and in improving the quality of services provided by the state.    3.1 State building    The fulfilment of these tasks, in turn, largely depends on the quantity and quality of civil servants and the efficiency of the public administration system.    I must say that recently attempts of all kinds of authorities, both in the centre and locally, to increase the number of state bodies have been intensified.    This is unacceptable.    Of course, life does not stand still and changes are needed somewhere. But the Government should proceed from a strict political commitment to prevent the growth of the total number of the state apparatus.    Exceptions are possible only where this is required by the state policy proclaimed by the President.    We have achieved a lot in forming a compact and professional Government. We should continue to improve the structure of the executive branch by abolishing unnecessary functions and links and decentralising the management process.    At the same time, it is necessary to strengthen the role and responsibility of ministries and agencies for the fulfilment of the functions entrusted to them.    In addition, it is time to actually start forming an "e-Government". This is a small government that is transparent in its activities. It will reduce contacts between the population and officials, improve the quality and reduce the time of service delivery. This will lead to a new administrative reform and reduction of the state apparatus.    To implement such work, a large programme to eliminate computer illiteracy and provide access to the Internet is needed.    I instruct the Government, I urge our citizens, especially young people, to work on computer self-education on a large scale, as was once the fight against illiteracy in the thirties of the last century.    Serious changes are required in the civil service, the system of training and retraining of civil servants in order to significantly improve the level of public administration and the quality of services provided by the state.    The activities of the Academy of Public Service must be fundamentally restructured, its material base must be strengthened and its financing must be ensured.    When accepting a position of a political servant, it is necessary to take into account the studies at the Academy.    A network of research centres should be developed at the Academy and the best teaching staff should be attracted to work there.    It is necessary to significantly increase the number of graduates of the Academy.    Since this year we have increased the salaries of civil servants by 50 per cent, and we will continue to work to improve the social protection of civil servants.    But with the growth of salaries, the requirements to civil servants themselves will also increase: their professionalism, patriotism, discipline, moral and ethical character.    Corruption offences must be severely prosecuted - the necessary legislation is in place.    Computer and Internet skills and preferably English language skills should be a mandatory requirement when hiring new civil servants, and in the future this requirement will also become compulsory.    It is necessary to toughen qualification requirements and make the work of attestation commissions more principled.    3.2 Internal policy    In the past and the current year, we will continue to work on further democratisation of our society within the framework of the five areas outlined in my address last year.    These remain valid, and in addition to them the following points should be emphasised.    We must focus on three fundamental elements: the development of civil society institutions, decentralisation, and the creation of a sustainable political-party system. Steps must be taken to strengthen stability, democracy and the protection of citizens' rights.    First, we should work on the introduction of new electoral mechanisms, clarifying the role and place of each subject of the political process.    We will further develop our party-political system by improving the legal norms governing the activities of parties and public associations.    The new legislation on the mass media and elections is now being discussed very actively in society. Critical remarks are being heard about them.    I would like to remind you that when we adopted legislative amendments concerning the number of parties of at least 50,000, this was called an insurmountable barrier.    But at the moment, nine parties have already been registered, which have easily overcome this barrier, and now no one questions the democracy of that amendment. This will also be the case with the current laws on the media and on elections.    The norms of the new electoral legislation are aimed at increasing professionalism and transparency in the work of election commissions at all levels.    It is also necessary to think about legally defining the powers of party factions in Parliament and local electoral bodies.    It is necessary to elaborate and adopt legal decisions on the issues of financing the activities of parties and NGOs by domestic legal entities and individuals. Support for the non-governmental sector should acquire a qualitatively new scale.    The issue of legal regulation of the activities of electoral blocs is also relevant.    Secondly, the potential of the permanent meeting on further democratisation of society has not yet been used to its full potential.    It is important that the Meeting becomes not only a "round table" where recommendations are made exclusively for the authorities.    The decisions taken at the PDS should be implemented by the parties through their representatives in Parliament and by NGOs through participation in specific socially significant projects.    Thirdly, in the autumn of this year, elections to the Majilis of the Parliament will be held, which will be a maturity test for political parties.    Our common duty is to ensure that the elections are held in strict compliance with the law.    3.3 Foreign policy and security    The active fight against terrorism has become a peculiarity of our time. The recent events in Russia and Spain have shocked everyone and made us think that perhaps there is not a single state protected from the barbaric actions of terrorists. Peaceful, innocent citizens are being killed.    That is why it is so important for us to consolidate regional and international efforts, in particular in the fight against international terrorism, religious extremism, drug trafficking and other contemporary challenges and threats to humanity.    Today Kazakhstan has stable, predictable relations with all neighbouring States.    A solid system of effective international co-operation has been established.    We are in favour of developing mutually beneficial bilateral relations with the countries of the East and West.    Kazakhstan's foreign policy should be oriented towards promoting the country's accelerated economic development and increasing its significance in the world.    Kazakhstan has declared itself a firm supporter of integration and multilateral co-operation.    In this regard, work should continue within the framework of the Common Economic Space, EurAsEC, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the CAC.    Russia is a very important country for Kazakhstan. We are in common geopolitical conditions and face common problems.    We have similar views on many processes in the world, and we need to realise them. The high level of economic integration and trust that has been achieved should be continued.    Kazakhstan highly values the achieved level of relations with the United States.    We are well aware of the importance of cooperation with America to ensure the development of a favourable external environment. Investments of American companies in Kazakhstan are an important factor of co-operation.    Of the $25 billion in foreign direct investment, the U.S. accounts for about $7.5 billion. We continue to look forward to broader co-operation, taking into account the interests of both sides.    Stable and friendly relations with our neighbour China are important. It is our reliable partner, with whom we are in constant dialogue on all issues of mutual interest. We need to work on increasing the volume of mutual trade. The high level of mutual understanding we have achieved will contribute to this.    Another, no less important, priority is the countries of Central Asia. We need to work more actively with our neighbours to bring their economies and, consequently, their countries and peoples closer together.    We also proceed from an understanding of the importance of ensuring stability on the southern borders of Kazakhstan.    The European Union is our largest trade and economic partner, and active work is needed here to promote and safeguard Kazakhstan's interests.    Our close relations with Turkey and the countries of the Islamic world must be kept under constant scrutiny.    The realisation of our plans, of course, also requires priority attention to the issues of ensuring Kazakhstan's security.    It is necessary to focus on the practical implementation of the initiative to consolidate the efforts of the CIS countries in combating new challenges and threats.    It is very important to continue the painstaking work to further realise the goals of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia.    Activities in the Collective Security Treaty Organisation should be adapted as much as possible to the emerging realities.    It is necessary to continue reforming the Armed Forces.    The main tasks facing the relevant State bodies are the professionalisation of the army and the improvement of its material and technical base.    We must pay attention to improving the manning system, planning the careers of servicemen, and creating a reserve. An important area of work should be the training of officer personnel at military institutes and military departments of the country's universities.    In order to improve the material and technical base of the army, it is necessary to take measures to optimise the quantity of weapons and military equipment.    * * *    In order to realise the tasks set out in this message, the Government and akims should provide for the necessary funding in the 2005 budget, as well as make appropriate proposals to clarify the current year's budget. The Parliament will have to adopt relevant laws.    * * *     Dear compatriots!
  We set ourselves challenging and seemingly difficult tasks, aimed at the future.    At the same time, let me remind you that fifteen years ago no one believed that Kazakhstan would turn from a peripheral union republic into an independent state with serious financial and intellectual resources.    Ten years ago, few believed that Kazakhstan would produce more than 50 million tonnes of oil (i.e. more than doubling its oil production), move its capital from Almaty to Astana, and be able to launch its own space satellite.    Five years ago, no one wanted to hear about the need to create a National Fund and a Development Bank.    Our own experience shows that life turns out to be bolder than plans.    As the French thinker Luc de Vauvenargue noted, "whoever is incapable of great achievements despises great plans".    We have already proved that Kazakhstan is ready for great achievements, and Kazakhstanis are capable of realising them.    Let us demonstrate it again!     Let us demonstrate that we can keep up with the times. We lagged far behind the world in our time and we do not want to be on the list of the last. We do not want to swallow the dust behind the departing train of world civilisation. And for this purpose we need all together to strain our forces, to collect in one fist all intellectual abilities of our people and to use its potential. I am sure that Kazakhstan will give birth to outstanding scientists capable of achieving high achievements. I am sure that medium-sized businesses will become stronger, create new jobs and work for the benefit of the whole country and all Kazakhstanis. Our Kazakhstan will grow rich and develop, and we will go steadfastly forward, as we ourselves have defined in the long-term development strategy of the country!

Title: Address of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Nursultan Nazarbayev, to the People of Kazakhstan
Full Text:
Our country continues to develop successfully in accordance with the long-term Strategy "Kazakhstan-2030" and the ten-year strategic plan.
We have achieved a lot in recent years. Kazakhstan's successes in market transformation, economic growth and improved living standards are well known and have been recognised by the international community.
Consistent measures have been taken to strengthen national security and internal political stability, further democratise society and develop regional cooperation.
Most importantly, we have a continuous and fruitful search for promising ways of sustainable development of society and the state, economy and social sphere.
This Address will outline the main directions of economic and social policy, further democratisation of society, development of cultural, educational and spiritual spheres in the next year, 2004.
I. Economic growth
Today Kazakhstan has developed fuel and energy, metallurgical and chemical complexes that ensure high rates of economic growth.
At the same time, we are facing the most important task of ensuring a balanced economy, advanced development of the processing industry, high-tech and knowledge-intensive industries, production infrastructure and the agro-industrial sector.
1.1 Agrarian policy
In last year's Address, I declared the years 2003-2005 to be the period of rural uplift.
The solution of the main tasks for the revival and development of agriculture and rural areas of the country will be the main content of the Government's socio-economic policy for the coming period.
For its effective implementation, a structural reorganisation of the public administration system has already been carried out.
During the past year, drafts of the Land, Water and Forest Codes, the Law "On Compulsory Insurance in Crop Production" were developed and submitted to the Parliament, the Laws "On Veterinary Medicine", "On Plant Protection", "On Seed Production" were adopted, amendments and additions were made to the Law "On Plant Quarantine".
In accordance with the approved programme documents, the state plans to invest more than 150 billion tenge in the rural economy in 2003-2005. Including in 2004 and 2005 with an increase of 10 billion tenge annually.
In the coming two years, an additional 30 billion tenge will be allocated for health care, 15 billion tenge each year. In addition, the state budget will allocate 15 billion tenge each year in 2004-2005 for investments in rural education, health care and rural water supply facilities.
In addition to the state agri-food programme, I intend to approve a state rural development programme this summer.
And, starting from 2004, the state will also allocate significant funds for its implementation.
The aim of this programme is to accelerate the social development of rural areas and to assist in the resettlement and employment of people from depressed, ecologically and economically unpromising rural areas.
I must recall that both the increased state support for the rural economy and the introduction of private land ownership are all being done to increase the share of the agricultural sector in the country's economy and, accordingly, to solve social problems in rural areas.
1.2 Industrial and innovation policy
While building a model of balanced and sustainable development, we must identify ways to diversify the economy from raw materials to processing.
Minerals, which Kazakhstan is rich in, are a non-renewable resource and the deposits are depleting over time. This could lead to a future loss of economic independence and then political independence.
Therefore, on my instruction, the Government has developed the Programme of Industrial and Innovative Development until 2015.
The main objective is to increase GDP by 3.5 times by this date compared to 2000.
The main goal of the programme is to create an entrepreneurial climate, a competitive environment, and a system of public institutions that will encourage the private sector to create high value-added industries.
In this respect, the country's ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy and the processing of raw materials, including agricultural raw materials, have significant potential for the creation of such industries.
The modern ways of organising such productions are such that they require state encouragement and the creation of high-tech centres.
It is necessary to skillfully use the existing scientific base by creating technoparks: in Alatau settlement near Almaty - an information technology centre, in Stepnogorsk - a biotechnology centre, in Kurchatov - a nuclear technology centre.
In implementing the programme, special attention will need to be paid to machine building, especially oil and gas, as well as transport development.
State support for the programme will consist of preferential loans, export insurance, equity participation in the founding capital, and dissemination of commercial information.
We plan that direct government expenditures of an investment nature will average 38 billion tenge ($250 million) per year. A significant part of these funds will be spent on the creation and modernisation of production and scientific infrastructure.
In this regard, there is a need to rethink our approaches to scientific and innovative practice.
The reform of science should concern not only structural changes, but also the volume of its financing. That is, the volume of state funding for scientific and applied research should be increased.
These tasks require a revision of the principles of foreign trade activity. It is already clear that the country should focus on trade liberalisation, linking it to regional integration, transition to world standards, and export-oriented production of goods and services.
In order to implement the Industrial and Innovative Development Programme, a system of development institutions will be created and capitalised.
These include the already existing National Fund, which has a savings and stabilisation function.
The Kazakhstan Investment Fund will be established in the near future. It is designed to facilitate the creation of Kazakhstani companies producing high value-added goods through equity participation.
In order to ensure continuous interaction between the scientific and technical and business spheres, an Innovation Fund will be established with broader powers to develop and implement innovations and venture entrepreneurship.
The Development Bank of Kazakhstan has already started its activities on lending to domestic enterprises operating in the non-resource sector of the economy, issuing loans for 23 billion tenge ($150 million). Its objective is to promote the development of the manufacturing industry and production infrastructure.
The government also needs to set up an Export Insurance Corporation to underwrite the political risks associated with international trade.
It should be emphasised that public development institutions will not replace or supplant the market, but will become the driving force of a competitive economy, involving private enterprises in innovation processes on the principles of partnership.
1.3 Integration policy
Our nation's integration initiatives will contribute to accelerated economic growth. As you know, Russia, Kazakhstan, Ukraine and Belarus, which make up more than 90 per cent of the total CIS economy, have recently announced the formation of a regional integration organisation. Our country will be a consistent supporter of the practical realisation of the goals of this association.
Much here will depend on the harmonisation of the legislative bases of our States and the active participation of parliamentarians in this process.
1.4 Investment Policy
I recall that in the current decade, in the socio-economic sphere, we have pledged to double the gross domestic product and to solve mainly the problem of poverty and unemployment.
In this regard, the main task for 2004 in the economic sphere is to achieve maximum economic growth rates.
This directly depends on the rapid growth of investment and an increase in the rate of accumulation in the gross domestic product.
In order to maintain sustainably high rates of economic growth, we need to bring the volume of gross fixed capital formation in relation to GDP to the level of 28 per cent over the next 4-5 years. This includes the growth of public investment from 2 to 4 per cent of GDP.
It is already evident that the state budget will be over-fulfilled this year and will approach the psychologically important level of one trillion tenge.
Therefore, there is a need to clarify the budget as early as May this year, and the excess revenues from the sale of stakes in large state-owned enterprises operating in strategic sectors of the economy should be directed to the National Fund.
In this regard, I instruct the Government to direct the surplus funds to both savings and social development when clarifying this year's budget in Parliament.
1.4.1 Public investments
In order to create and capitalise the above-mentioned financial institutions ensuring the implementation of the industrial-innovation programme, I propose to direct:
- to increase the authorised capital of the Development Bank and fill its credit resources - 12 billion tenge;
- into the authorised capital of the Kazakhstan Investment Fund to be established - 23 billion tenge;
- to the Innovation Fund to be established - 3 billion tenge;
- for the establishment of the Export Insurance Corporation - 7.7 billion tenge.
1.4.2 Development of Astana
Nowadays, almost no one doubts the strategic necessity and expediency of moving the capital to the centre of the country and its arrangement in a modern style.
Having started to realise great plans to improve the architectural appearance of our capital, we should not and cannot afford not to bring this matter to the end.
We have spoken many times about the economic, political and social benefits of building a new capital of the country.
Thus, over the years of creation and development of Astana, about 2.5 billion dollars from various sources have been invested in its development, which has contributed to the economic growth of the country, revitalisation of production, creation of jobs and increase in tax revenues.
All regional centres of the country have been transformed following the example of Astana. The programme "The Prosperity of Astana - the Prosperity of Kazakhstan" is in effect.
We are grateful to friendly countries, our foreign investors, and domestic entrepreneurs who make significant contributions to the construction of the capital.
With the grant funds they provided at my request, they are building facilities worth about $200 million this year alone.
But in the future we need to move to planned construction of the capital at the expense of budget funds, based on long-term and medium-term plans and programmes of its development.
The Government, together with the Astana Akimat, should ensure that the construction of social and cultural facilities is carried out as planned.
1.4.3 Private investment
The private sector should play an increasing role in our economy. Let me remind you that today the total capital of the pension accumulation system is approaching 300 billion tenge. Deposits in the banking system have exceeded 600 billion.
The total equity capital of banks increased by more than a third over the year and exceeded a billion dollars, while loans to the economy have increased 4.5 times over the past three years.
All of this, of course, ensures and sustains high economic growth rates.
But we are interested in much greater growth in private savings and savings, and most importantly, investment in the economy.
1.5 Tax policy
It may be considered an immutable truth that the lower the taxes, the more private investment.
I am therefore instructing the Government to submit to Parliament a proposal to further reduce the rates of certain taxes.
I believe that as of 1 January 2004 we need to:
- reduce the value added tax rate from 16 per cent to 15 per cent;
- reduce the social tax rate by differentiating it from 20 to 7 per cent depending on the level of employers' labour costs on a regressive scale;
- reduce the maximum individual income tax rate from 30 per cent to 20 per cent.
I instruct the Government, taking into account the positive experience of small businesses operating under simplified taxation, to study the possibility of expanding the scope of special tax regimes.
II. Social development
By increasing the rate of economic growth, we are not only strengthening the country's economic power, but also creating ever greater opportunities for addressing the challenges of social development.
The most important element of this policy is to further increase pensions and wages.
2.1 Pensions
I consider it necessary to increase the level of minimum pension to 5.5 thousand tenge.
I am sure that the time has come, and the country has the opportunity, to establish a fairer scale of pensions, taking into account the labour contribution of each pensioner, his length of service, and the salary from which he retired.
This will enable nearly one million pensioners to increase their pensions.
We must begin to solve this difficult and rather expensive, but noble task immediately. I instruct the Government to implement a differentiated increase in pensions: to recalculate them from 1 June this year, and to start paying them from 1 July. And the new minimum pension should also start to be paid from 1 July.
Calculations show that for this purpose it is necessary to allocate additional 60 billion tenge over a year and a half, including about 20 billion tenge already this year.
As a result, the average size of pensions next year should exceed the level of eight thousand tenge.
2.2 Wages
The minimum wage this year has reached the level of the minimum pension, although it should exceed it.
It will therefore be increased from 5,000 to 6,600 tenge, or 32 per cent, from 1 January next year.
In previous years, we have increased wages for employees of budget-funded institutions. Last year, teachers alone received a salary increase of more than 35 per cent.
In connection with the continuation of an active social policy, starting next year the wages of public sector employees will be increased by another 20 per cent on average. At the same time, it is planned to further improve the labour remuneration system.
At the same time, under the new remuneration system being developed, civil servants' salaries will increase by an average of 50 per cent.
At the same time, the Government should clarify the wage grid, and first of all, to ensure that the increase affects low-paid workers.
Overall, more than 50 billion tenge will be allocated from the state budget for wage increases in 2004.
In addition, in order to support low-income people, I instruct the Government to increase the non-taxable minimum for individual income tax when reducing taxes by at least 30 per cent.
These measures will improve the well-being of the majority of Kazakhstan's low-income population and will be an important factor in significantly reducing unemployment.
Another important issue. We need to think seriously about making up for our country's migration losses. This is a serious problem on the solution of which the realisation of our plans depends.
Therefore, the Government should develop a programme that includes:
- increased fertility,
- Reducing mortality by improving health care,
- increasing the intake of immigrants, primarily from among former Kazakhstanis of working age.
On this basis, I also set a task for next year to double the quota for oralmans, allocating an additional two billion tenge for this purpose.
2.3 Safeguarding cultural and historical heritage
As an essential component of the development of the spiritual and educational sphere, I propose to develop and launch this year a special medium-term programme "Cultural Heritage", which would include a number of large-scale projects.
Her goal:
Firstly, to create a holistic system for studying the vast cultural heritage of the people, including contemporary national culture, folklore, traditions and customs.
Secondly, to ensure the recreation of significant historical, cultural and architectural monuments of particular importance to national history.
Thirdly, to generalise the centuries-old experience of national literature and writing and to create detailed artistic, scientific, biographical series.
Fourth, to create in the state language a full-fledged fund of humanitarian education based on the best achievements of world scientific thought, culture and literature.
Among the measures for cultural and spiritual development, special attention should be paid to the development of the cultural environment of our capital city.
I instruct the Government, with the participation of the Presidential Administration, to prepare a decision on this matter within three months.
* * *
All the measures I have proposed, especially with regard to social development and the need for savings to sustain high economic growth, are balanced and in line with our capabilities.
Therefore, I appeal to the members of Parliament to support these proposals. They will undoubtedly significantly improve the well-being of a significant part of the citizens of our country.
III. Democratisation and good governance
Kazakhstanis know that we are consistently moving towards an open society according to the principle: first the economy, then politics.
We know other things, too.
If the country's management had been lost in the early 90s, then in the years of severe crisis and in the conditions of a multinational country, we could have lost the state and failed to solve the tasks of reforming the economy. There are real examples of this. But we state that we have succeeded.
What we have achieved in the economy and State-building now allows us to focus more deeply on further liberalisation of the political system.
This will be the next stage in the development of civil society, taking into account our realities.
Today we have formed key institutions of democracy and civil society.
Only recently has the institution of an ombudsman been established, and the National Council and the Public Council for the Mass Media have been set up.
The Government has a standing meeting to elaborate proposals for further democratisation and the development of civil society.
After the adoption of the new law on parties, the party system in the country is being strengthened, non-governmental organisations are becoming more active and, most importantly, a democratic type of political culture is being established in society.
Consistently implementing our policy in this direction, we have further steps to take on this path.
I propose a programme of political reforms for the coming period, including five priority areas.
One.
We need to modernise the system of public administration. Its main tasks are clear delineation of competence between the levels of state administration, improvement of the system of inter-budget relations.
At the meeting of the National Council held yesterday, we considered amendments and additions to the Local Government Act.
They are associated with further expansion of the powers of local public administration in addressing issues of territorial development, organisation of effective management at lower levels, primarily in rural areas.
And for this purpose it is necessary to make amendments and additions to almost 150 laws. Therefore, I have set a task for the Government to prepare by the beginning of 2004 the relevant amendments to the legislative and legal framework to ensure the effective functioning of all levels of government.
The draft of the Budget Code is being finalised, which the Government is obliged to submit to the Parliament in May this year.
Therefore, I would like to ask the deputies to study it carefully and adopt it this year, so that next year we can start forming the budget for 2005 on the basis of the new Budget Code.
And the draft law on the republican budget for 2004 will be developed on the basis of the norms of the current Law "On the Budget System".
Once we finalise the work on defining the powers of the levels of government and their financial support, the logical conclusion of this process will be to expand the practice of electing heads of local executive bodies.
Our main task is to make local authorities more responsible to people, closer to everyday problems and concerns of a particular person.
I believe that at the level of rural districts it is possible to introduce the election of akims for a certain period of time.
Then an experiment with the election of district akims should be conducted. Based on its results, it will be necessary to determine the expediency of this practice and the most optimal model.
But it should be remembered that the election of akims is not an end in itself. This issue should be solved step by step, as the necessary conditions are created.
I also believe it is necessary to immediately begin creating conditions for training personnel at all levels of government. Studying at the best universities in the world, creating elite universities in the country, and strengthening the national Academy of Public Service are today's tasks.
We will move step by step, preserving the values of our culture, unity, inter-ethnic and inter-confessional harmony, and political stability. I never tire of repeating this.
But at the same time, one should always be aware that no country has reached perfection in the state and political structure, no one has built ideal inter-budget relations.
Even in developed civilised countries, the stages of liberalisation and decentralisation are followed by a sharp strengthening of the role of the state and centralisation: it all depends on specific historical conditions and the objectivity of the stages of development.
It should be well understood that attempts to copy other people's experience, as one international expert aptly put it, are akin to organ transplant surgery, when, as you know, there is a strong reaction of rejection.
In such matters you have to be careful and weigh everything carefully.
I instruct the Government to study this issue in depth, taking into account similar foreign experience, and to make specific proposals.
Second.
The electoral system should be further improved. The electoral process should become even more transparent and open.
As early as last year, on my instruction, a draft law "On Amendments and Additions to the Constitutional Law "On Elections in the Republic of Kazakhstan" was developed.
It takes into account the recommendations of round tables held with political parties by the CEC in co-operation with the OSCE. Earlier this year, the draft law was discussed at meetings of the Standing Meeting.
The Government should finalise it, taking into account the comments and suggestions made by the public, and submit it to Parliament.
The main goal of this law should be transparency, openness and competitiveness of electoral processes.
An automated information system for compiling voter lists, voting, tabulation of results and determination of election results should be introduced.
Third.
An important direction in the democratisation of the political system is the further strengthening of civil society institutions.
Our task is to promote the existence of strong and responsible parties that enjoy mass support and high credibility. This is in the strategic interests of the country.
I consider it necessary for political parties to be given the exclusive right to nominate candidates for deputies to the Majilis, while retaining the institution of self-nomination.
Parties should also have a greater ability to exercise control over the tabulation of results.
Interaction with non-governmental organisations needs to be structured differently.
I believe that the practice of economic support of NGOs through the system of state social order on a competitive basis would be productive.
For this purpose, it is necessary to accelerate the preparation and adoption of the draft laws "On Non-Governmental Organisations in the Republic of Kazakhstan" and "On State Social Order".
This work has been unnecessarily delayed.
The Government needs to finalise these draft laws and submit them to Parliament.
A civic forum - a nationwide congress of NGOs - should initiate large-scale co-operation. It should be held in the second half of this year.
Fourth.
We must define precisely the role and place of the media in the process of democratisation of our society.
Over the years of independence, Kazakhstan has created the political, economic and legal conditions for the functioning of independent mass media. This is a reality confirmed by legislative and regulatory acts.
The vast majority of media outlets are non-state.
But this is not the crux of the matter, but the real mechanism for the functioning of the press and television, when there is no censorship, when favourable mechanisms have been created for the work of the mass media, and when the legal mechanism for their activities is clearly defined. There are serious resources of financial support for the mass media, which the state has been actively using over the past year. By the way, more than 50 new media outlets have already been registered this year alone.
This is the height that the state and the journalistic community have reached together.
And this is a major gain, the importance of which cannot be overemphasised.
But we must think about new directions for the development of the media space. We are talking about the mutual responsibility of society and the media, of the authorities and journalists.
This problem exists not only in Kazakhstan, but in all modern societies. Recent events make it clear that the interests of national security, political stability, inter-ethnic consensus, and confessional peace are becoming a priority not only at the state level, but also at the interstate level.
As we have seen, under certain conditions, the media of even the most democratic states choose a clear position in defence of national interests. We should not become an exception.
There is a need to adopt a new media law that would take into account the current realities of ensuring freedom of expression, as well as the protection of journalists from ownership pressure and toughen the responsibility of officials for interfering in the activities of a free press.
On the other hand, it is also necessary to clearly define the responsibility of the media for violations of laws. Society demands freedom of speech, not freedom of slander and disinformation.
The Government, together with journalists and the public, should draft and introduce a bill to Parliament this year.
The government should clearly monitor the processes of competition in the media market, suppressing and preventing its monopolisation.
The media are becoming mature, understanding the interests of the country, and thus their own interests. And, I hope, they will respond to the concern for their development with a responsible stance, consisting in the dissemination of objective information.
These are axioms that everyone must internalise for the simple reason that there is simply no other mechanism.
The leaders of the dialogue between the authorities and the media can and should be, first and foremost, public associations of journalists and the Public Council on Mass Media under the President of the country.
Fifth.
One of the main problems remains the improvement of the work of law enforcement and judicial bodies. I believe that this problem should be considered first and foremost from the perspective of ensuring the protection of the inalienable rights and freedoms of citizens.
It is important to continue the further humanisation of the field of criminal law.
In order to introduce a moratorium on the death penalty, it is time for the Government to begin to create the organisational, material and legislative conditions for dealing with this issue, in particular by introducing a form of punishment such as life imprisonment.
Practice shows that the attention and care of the state to the needs of the judiciary should be accompanied by an increase in the demanding behaviour of the judiciary.
Citizens still do not see the court as a tool to protect their rights and restore justice.
We need to think about the phased introduction of the institution of jurors.
Legal levers to control the activities of the courts should also be strengthened, without, of course, interfering with the administration of justice.
It is necessary to improve the quality of professional training of judges. It may be advisable to create a special training magistracy. As a rule, only those who have graduated from it should become judges.
In accordance with the Constitution, judicial control over the procedural activities of criminal prosecution bodies should be strengthened, up to and including the introduction of the institution of judicial authorisation of arrest.
It is also necessary to establish simplified and accelerated procedures both at the stage of pre-trial consideration of a case and in court instances.
* * *
Dear Kazakhstanis!
Honourable parliamentarians!
You remember that in the most difficult years, I never promised the people "golden mountains" or made populist statements, but always honestly warned that difficulties and hardships of reforms awaited us, which would fall on the shoulders of ordinary people. But I convinced people that time would come and the living standards of the people would steadily rise.
In the shortest historical period of time, we have carried out the fastest economic and political reforms. We ourselves, our thinking and world outlook have changed. We understood without much prompting that only our own labour will be the source of prosperity, and the state must create legal conditions for this.
Today I can responsibly say that I am fulfilling what I promised. The growth of Kazakhstan's economy serves our main goal - the growth of people's well-being.
I've been talking about this time, and now it's here.
I have the honour of announcing the largest increases in social spending in our recent history, which we will begin soon and which will affect every Kazakhstani and every family.
For these purposes, over 120 billion tenge will be allocated from the state treasury over a year and a half, which is not comparable to previous years.
If the economy performs as well as it has, this trend will continue, as envisaged in the long-term Strategy "Kazakhstan-2030".
Today, unlike in the past, we have development and improvement programmes in place for the four core pillars on which our economy is based:
- agri-food programme;
- industrial innovation programme;
- infrastructure and energy development;
- social development programmes.
Today, unlike in past years, we also have the necessary financial resources available.
It is a matter of well-coordinated work of all branches of government, effective laws and their implementation.
And our cohesion and creative energy, the desire to preserve stability, civil and national harmony, to ensure peace and tranquillity in the country will be the main guarantee of Kazakhstan's progressive advancement towards prosperity and well-being.

Title: Address of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Nursultan Nazarbayev, to the People of Kazakhstan
Full Text:
ON THE MAIN DIRECTIONS OF DOMESTIC AND FOREIGN POLICY FOR 2003
Dear deputies!   Dear compatriots!
Quite recently, you and I summarised the ten-year development of our state. It was not just a report on what has been achieved, but also a wealth of historical material for posterity. It was a critical analysis of the degree of our maturity, readiness to say goodbye to the past and open a new historical stage of development of independent Kazakhstan.
At the same time, we have once again seen that we have travelled a great distance on the path of development and have reached the point where we can enter the twenty-first century without hesitation.
The main outcome of our endeavours over these years is that our republic has emerged as an independent and self-sufficient state, as an equal partner of the world community. We have carried out energetic, tough, but significant results of targeted economic reforms.
The fact that Kazakhstan is recognised by both the European Union and the United States as a market economy speaks volumes.
We have also made significant progress in nation-building and the development of democracy. Our country and all of Kazakhstan's society have changed dramatically: economic and political rights and freedoms have become an indisputable fact of our reality.
All of these outcomes and changes are a solid foundation for today's day.
At the same time, we have never fallen into euphoria or glossed over our problems, as I noted in my anniversary report. We have yet to pass the stage of maturation and maturity of the State and the establishment of Kazakhstan's civil society. Both the political system and the issues of citizens' rights and freedoms require continuous improvement in accordance with the level of economic and socio-cultural development.
This is the focus of our ten-year plan based on the Kazakhstan-2030 Strategy.
* * *
In order to continue to work dynamically on building socio-economic capacity, it is crucial to define precisely the medium-term plans and priorities for the medium term and 2003.
I have approved a three-year Programme of Action of the Government, in which the main emphasis is placed on solving the problems of improving the structure of the real sector of the economy, developing the transport infrastructure, raising the living standards of the population, and further integrating the country's economy into regional common markets.
That is why I would like to set out specific accents and priorities in my message, which will enable the Government to translate its intentions into concrete budget programmes.
I believe it is necessary and logical, firstly, to move away from the practice of declaring each year as the year of a particular sphere or area of activity and move to prioritising three years.
Secondly, for the first time the President's Address to the people of Kazakhstan is voiced during the budgeting process, rather than after its completion, as it was before.
* * *
Dear compatriots!
There are a number of reasons to devote the coming period, from 2003 to 2005, to the revival of the aul (village).
It is to this problem that my message is dedicated.
It must be recognised that it was agriculture and its workers who suffered the most from the imperfections of the Soviet economy, and it was they who felt the full extent of its damage during the transition to the market.
The village is a way of life of the people, a source of culture, traditions, customs and spiritual life. This set of factors alone requires us to take the village seriously.
It is well known and proven by history that in any revolutionary cataclysms the main burden of painful changes falls on the village. And Kazakhstan was not an exception.
We must remember that it is the rural population that is the genetic embodiment of any nation. It is they who are most eager for stability and sound evolutionary development.
And it is it that most keenly and subtly perceives the ideals of independence and strong statehood, because at the genetic-informational level it keeps and reproduces the aspirations and hopes of our ancestors.
But there are also purely economic reasons. A careful review of the internal structure of the economy, nearby and distant markets makes one think seriously about deepening Kazakhstan's agro-industrial specialisation.
Paradoxically, but the fact is that all neighbouring and distant markets are in need of food, primarily grain and meat. But Kazakhstani food cannot get there due to low quality and high costs, weak state and diplomatic support.
Moreover, the domestic market is already starting to lose out to the growing expansion of food imports in a number of areas.
It is also extremely important that a strong agricultural sector in the country would help to substantially boost its associated industries: mineral fertiliser production, agricultural machinery, light and food industries, and others along the technological chain. This means that the multiplier effect for the country's economy will be enormous.
It is impossible not to mention the demographic, migration and social factors of our special attitude to the aul.
In Kazakhstan, historically, especially in the era of the command economy, the settlement of people in rural areas has been unsuccessful both from the standpoint of the market economy and for social and environmental reasons.
As a result, many rural areas have been characterised by depressed economies.
We can definitely say that about one million people live under minimum standards of self-sufficiency both in terms of land quality, natural and social conditions.
We must analyse one peculiarity in the most serious way. Kazakhstan has a rural population of 43 per cent. From the oversupply of the rural population, unemployment is high in many areas, which in turn undermines rural labour markets, reducing them to the lowest level in the country.
All this leads to a mass outflow of rural population to district centres and cities. In 2000-2001, 186 unpromising and therefore abandoned settlements were abolished, and another 93 are expected to be abolished this year.
This phenomenon, however painful it may be perceived by us and the population, should be seen as an objective process.
The only problem is that it is spontaneous in our country and does not depend on the executive branch.
In ten years, we have stood on our feet as a state with a good position in the economy. Now it is time to build on what we have achieved and the experience we have accumulated, to help our compatriots living in rural areas find a new quality of life through concrete actions.
What exactly am I suggesting.
First. Everyone needs to clearly understand that support to the village should not and will not consist in widespread state subsidies and irrevocable financing of everything and anything. We cannot and will not revive the former practice of dependency and state paternalism.
It is necessary to continue to purposefully pursue the line of creating conditions for people to earn money for themselves and their families, it is necessary to support those who can and can work and show their diligence. This is the responsibility of the state to the people and their future.
All financial and economic policy of the state, including social and agricultural policy, should be selectively directed only to those territories that are promising from the point of view of human life and market functioning.
Second. I instruct the Government to develop a model for resettlement of residents of rural areas for the future. The fate of a number of depressed small towns must also be decided decisively.
The country needs a state policy to encourage internal migration from unpromising regions to developing regions, district centres and small towns. It should take into account the issues of planning and management of migration flows, settlement, provision of land and housing, and retraining of migrants.
All people aspire to live in an ecologically clean environment, to have access to good social services. This aspiration should be supported. It is obvious that the village has a chance for a normal life where there is good land, where there are markets nearby, where transport communications are convenient.
There is also a question of giving the Ministry of Agriculture additional functions of territorial affairs.
Third. I set a task for the Government to develop a three-year presidential programme for the development of Kazakhstan's agro-industrial complex as soon as possible.
Our country has traditionally been and must remain a global and regional supplier of food, and the agro-industrial complex itself is an additional source of economic growth, improving the country's balance of trade and balance of payments. And we must make every effort to achieve this.
Sustainable and dynamic development of the agro-industrial complex and the rapid rise of its economy on modern market principles remain the main factor of rural uplift.
Here I would emphasise the following key points.
It is necessary to bring to a logical conclusion the reform of economic, and first of all, land and water relations.
We must admit that the recently adopted Law on Land has not moved the country towards a civilised market. And if we have collectively made mistakes, let us quickly correct them and amend this law. The cornerstone of this law should be the answer to the vital question: "Is private ownership of agricultural land necessary?".
When answering this question, we usually fall back on the philistine thesis - "selling the Motherland", without realising that private land ownership is, first and foremost, a peasant's confidence that his land will not be taken away. Ownership of land is a motivation to develop it so that there is something to pass on to one's children.
Land without an owner is an orphan. Ecological catastrophe catches up precisely on the no man's land. In the conditions of Kazakhstan - inclusion in the economy of huge resources that have not yet been used.
I am confident that this Parliament will be able to fulfil this historic mission by adopting the Law on Private Land Ownership.
I instruct the Government, having studied the experience of other countries and weighed up all the pros and cons, to develop and submit a draft of this law to Parliament.
Finally, it is time to restore order in water relations, where organisational and legal confusion also reigns. It is necessary to consistently solve the overripe problem of reconstruction of irrigation and drainage facilities.
Medium- and large-scale crop and livestock production oriented towards exports and large-scale domestic public procurement should be initiated, including economic measures.
It is necessary to provide state assistance on a repayable but preferential basis to ensure rapid growth of labour productivity and reduction of production costs in agriculture.
It is important to use economic methods to encourage farmers to introduce modern agricultural technologies, develop agricultural processing industries and create at least equal economic conditions for Kazakh producers with neighbouring countries.
It is time to strengthen and seriously improve state control and supervision of product quality.
The government should put in order the system of veterinary and sanitary supervision, animal and plant disease control, fundamentally improve work with standards and technological norms, quickly and consistently bringing them closer to the world standards.
It is necessary to restore scientific and information support of the village. Agricultural institutes should work in the system of the Ministry of Agriculture, and the Agency for Statistics should seriously deal with the problem of primary information. Akims at all levels should be assisted in deploying the information and marketing system, which is still functioning only in 36 districts.
The government should take effective measures to expand foreign markets.
The organisation of transport routes to foreign markets, as well as excessive tariff and non-tariff burdens on trade routes leave much to be desired.
Rural areas need a more extensive financial network for the provision of credit and financial services in the form of various microcredit and mutual credit institutions.
It is necessary to get serious about insurance of agricultural production.
The Government should continue the practice of channelling a significant part of external loans on favourable and soft terms to agriculture, especially through international banks. It is necessary to strengthen the capacity of leasing centres and credit partnerships.
Fourth. I instructed the Government to pay special attention to the social sphere.
And here a new rural policy should take an important place. This policy of developing promising regions naturally needs sufficient financial support.
First of all, we should not interfere with the peasant, give him the freedom to raise his farm independently, help him in crediting, consulting, selling his products.
The budget of these three years should be prioritised for the village. Of the funds directed to the social sphere, emphasise the village: roads and water pipelines - first of all for the village; hospitals - first of all for the needs of the village; schools - first of all for the village. I instruct the Government and akims to increase annually during 2003-2005 the amount of funding for rural education, health care, funds for drinking water and for the construction and reconstruction of inter-oblast and inter-district rural roads by 10 billion tenge.
But it should be a well-considered investment: for example, why build new schools in depressed areas where the population is declining? In such cases, it is necessary to build boarding schools in promising areas and transfer children to them. The same applies to modern hospitals.
In addition, up to 8-10 billion tenge should be allocated annually for agricultural development from 2003 onwards.
I consider it a strategic task to fundamentally change things in the education system. The key importance for the country is a significant increase in the status of the teacher, and first of all the rural teacher. First of all, it is necessary to solve the issue of teachers' remuneration.
I believe it is possible to increase teachers' salaries by more than 30 per cent already this year, rather than by 25 per cent as previously planned.
I instruct the Government and Akims to find the necessary financial sources for this purpose.
Fifth. The migration strategy, special emphasis on rural areas and the social sphere will apparently require some budget decentralisation.
But here both the Government and the Parliament need to be balanced and restrained until a model of rural settlement is developed, bearing in mind that it will inevitably lead to a certain administrative-territorial reorganisation at the level of rural districts and districts.
And lastly. It is necessary to take a whole set of measures to legalise property, more specifically land and immovable property of rural migrants in cities and small entrepreneurs.
Because the property of this circle of people is illegal or semi-legal, not properly registered, it cannot be capitalised, sold or pledged. It falls out of both the legal accounting system and the new economic relations.
This is a huge potential. World experts believe that most poor countries already have the assets and resources that can give these countries a breakthrough.
We are in a transit zone of economic development. Expert economists estimate that 25 to 35% of the assets and resources of economic growth, including small and medium-sized businesses, are in illegal circulation.
Their inclusion in the market turnover will have a huge effect on the entire economy of the country.
On this basis, it is necessary to strengthen small and medium-sized businesses in every possible way, addressing the following key tasks step by step:
- reducing the tax burden;
- legalisation of property and assets;
- facilitating access to credit resources;
- simplification of administrative procedures and authorisations;
- protection from bureaucratic arbitrariness and control and verification bodies;
- Establishment of regional SME support centres, assistance in market research, professional development, creation of a centralised accounting office.
I instruct the Government to set up a special commission on these issues.
Responsibility for fulfilment of the set tasks on rural development requires responsible and coordinated work of the Government and akims. It can be considered as a test for the whole system of executive power.
In this message, I have deliberately emphasised one but crucial issue in our new rural policy. The Government and the Budget Commission must adequately identify the relevant priorities for the next year.
At the same time, I would like to highlight a number of issues related to the main directions of State-building and democratisation of society.
A set of relevant measures for the medium term has been approved. It is based on the inviolability of the Basic Law and the inviolability of the constitutional order.
In the opinion of many experts, including international ones, the Constitution of Kazakhstan adopted in 1995 is inherently democratic and meets the needs of the country's development.
The potential of this Basic Law has not yet been realised in many respects. I support this position. Unity, inter-ethnic harmony and political stability are the main things our people want. I know it.
Democracy is our consciously chosen path of development, which I have offered you and which you have accepted. And we must all work to deepen this process, relying on the wisdom of the people, taking into account historical, economic, political, ethno-social factors and public opinion.
We will move step by step, preserving the values of our culture, which is based on mutual assistance, tolerance, collectivism, and mutual respect between people of different nationalities. Other people's recipes can harm us.
We will strengthen the efforts of the state and society in strictly observing the rights and freedoms of citizens, and we will take concrete actions to combat bureaucratic arbitrariness both in the centre and on the ground.
We have a lot of reserves for improving party and political construction, first of all, its legislative framework. Such issues as the introduction of legal norms preventing political extremism in the activities of parties, the exclusion of party building on ethnic or confessional principles, and ensuring financial transparency in their activities are long overdue.
In this respect, I support the initiative of a group of MPs to change party legislation.
The Government should also initiate the drafting of a law on the status and rights of non-governmental organisations.
We will continue to persistently and vigorously work to improve nation-building, develop local public administration and self-government, and improve the judicial and electoral systems.
On my instructions, the Government is working on the preparation of a Concept for the delineation of powers between levels of government and the improvement of intergovernmental fiscal relations.
As a result of this work, a draft of an optimal list of state functions and their delimitation by levels of government should be prepared. It will become the basis for creating the basic conditions for the transition to new principles of state administration and an appropriate model of inter-budget relations by the beginning of 2004.
It is necessary to solve the issues of transferring some powers and responsibilities from the centre to the regions. Then the structure of power itself will become clear, it will be clear where to elect and where to appoint the head.
One of the objectives of the concept is the formation of full-fledged institutions of state power at the rural level of government.
In rural areas there is a certain power vacuum. Local akims do not have sufficient authority and, most importantly, financial resources. Therefore, the Government and regional akims should organise effective public administration at the lower levels.
In August of this year, a detailed analysis of the experiment on election of akims of rural districts will be carried out, and on its basis a decision will be made on the expediency of electing this category of leaders by the population.
At the same time, it is necessary to determine how many levels of government we should have. And only after defining all the fundamental principles of state governance, it will be possible to approach the model and the law on local self-governance.
This year serious changes will be made to the Law on Civil Service. These include a transition from a competitive to a career system of promotion through the ranks of the civil service, as well as the elimination of all the distortions in the current law.
Measures will be taken to improve personnel policy in the courts and limit corruption in the judiciary, and to strengthen the role of the Bar in the human rights mechanism. By the end of the year, a concept for introducing the institution of jury trials will be developed.
The question of introducing a moratorium on the death penalty, up to and including its complete abolition, should be seriously explored. I realise that conditions must be created for this to happen. This requires funding and time. I know that there are different opinions in society. But we need to start solving this problem.
There are also a number of measures to improve the performance of the media.
In the near future, the composition of the tender commission for the distribution of radio frequencies will be revised and expanded to include public representatives. A public council on information policy under the head of state is being set up.
In its development, our statehood is gradually approaching the point where Parliament should make fuller use of its powers granted by the Constitution, including with regard to the Government.
Constant dialogue between the Parliament and the Government, joint legislative work is the most important condition for strengthening statehood.
The solution of serious tasks is envisaged for the next year as well. Among them are the introduction of amendments and additions to the Constitutional Law "On the Government", the legislative introduction of the mechanism of the state social order for the services of non-governmental organisations, the development of the draft law "On Alternative Military Service" and others.
In conclusion, I would like to make a number of fundamental points about our foreign policy. Life and practice confirm that from the very beginning we have chosen the right line of behaviour in the international arena.
The decision to give up nuclear weapons still works for the security and positive image of our country.
Kazakhstan is one of the few states in the post-Soviet space that has managed to build good stable relations with all countries without damaging its strategic interests.
From now on, we will pursue precisely such a multilateral pragmatic policy, which is fully in line with Kazakhstan's geopolitical location and economic potential. Such a policy is the key to strengthening our national security.
At the same time, we must make even greater efforts to strengthen the factors of predictability and stability in Kazakhstan's relations with neighbouring states.
Our diplomacy should pay the most serious attention to strengthening such priority organisations as EurAsEC, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the Central Asian Cooperation Organisation.
At the same time, we will develop co-operation with the USA, Western Europe and other countries.
Concrete results should be achieved on the convening of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia.
It is necessary to strengthen our foreign economic policy by merging the efforts of the state and private business in gaining a strong position in foreign markets.
Kazakhstan, having built a market economy, has become an integral part of the globalisation process.
It is essential that we find our place in the world, to carefully strategise our future actions to avoid costs and, on the contrary, to reap dividends.
In this regard, the Government should seriously intensify its preparations for accession to the World Trade Organisation.
* * *
The questions raised in this message are dictated by life itself. Many of them you yourself have raised in meetings with me, and they are being raised by people.
Every year more and more activities of the state and society are regulated by laws. Therefore, both the Parliament and the Government need to consult more with those who have to live by these laws.
You can't solve everything at once, you need to be tolerant, don't scatter over small things, focus on the chosen priorities.
We, as people's elected representatives of the executive and representative branches of government, must be balanced and guided by reason, not emotion, when addressing important public issues.
And I look forward to your support in implementing the provisions of this message.
Thank you for your attention.

Title: Address of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Nursultan Nazarbayev, to the People of Kazakhstan
Full Text:
On the Situation in the Country and Main Directions of Domestic and Foreign Policy for 2002

Dear deputies! Dear citizens of Kazakhstan!

We can say for certain that the life has proved correctness of our choice of the model of open market economy and democratic development.

It is very important that our reforms have been socially oriented. This has allowed to avoid large political cataclysms that have taken place in other countries that started reforming.

Now many facts of our life are meant as standing to reason, including freedom of business undertakings and trade, tax, budget and bank systems, private enterprises, farms and many others.

But eight or ten years ago there was nothing of all this and even the ideas were perceived by no means unambiguously. It is enough to remember the debates in the society and accusations about the authorities.

Public conscience changed with great difficulties.

However, we have overcome all this. We have laid the foundation for new economic relationship and created market mechanisms almost from nothing.

Now the economy of the country is on rise as GDP grew over 14 percent during the first half of the year related to the same period of the last year. Production is restored and reconstructed, and the country is rising.

Agricultural production has grown by over 5 percent on the results of the first half of the year. Interest-free credits organized by the state promoted good sowing campaign and start of harvesting.
